info.bio: Fugazi – "Fucked Up, Got Ambushed, Zipped In", acrónimo utilizado por los soldados en Vietnam para describir una situación muy comprometida- se formó en 1987 en Washington, siendo inicialmente un trío (Ian McKaye, Brendan Canty y Joe Lally) que se reunía para tocar en directo. Posteriormente se les une Guy Picciotto, y con la formación que siguen manteniendo graban sus primeros Eps (Fugazi en 1988 y Margin Walker en 1989) en Dischord, combativo sello fundado por McKaye y que sigue dirigiendo hoy en día.

scenes.name: Cruces del punk: de Fugazi al punk-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el punk es el más vivo de los subgéneros del rock: miles de bandas ensayando en garajes, un lenguaje universal como no se veía desde los sesenta. Nueva York: Adrenalin O.D., el straight-edge de Youth Of Today y Gorilla Biscuits, el crossover punk-metal (Cro-Mags, Prong, Danzig). Washington lanza a Pussy Galore (la irrelevancia hecha relevante), Unrest y Fugazi de Ian MacKaye, que abstrae el hardcore en una forma teatral de compromiso ético y estético (Repeater, Steady Diet Of Nothing, Red Medicine), y Royal Trux (Twin Infinitives, «un Trout Mask Replica para la generación grunge»). El punk-pop de Mr T Experience, Dwarves, Henry Rollins, L7 (pioneras del «foxcore»), Lemonheads, Screeching Weasel, Goo Goo Dolls, Fastbacks, Shonen Knife; el «rogue folk» de los Pogues, Membranes y Chumbawamba.

podcast.title: Fan Letter from Teenage Dave Grohl (1983)
podcast.body: In approximately 1983, when he was 14, Dave Grohl sent a fan letter to Ian MacKaye, a member of Fugazi, expressing appreciation for their "Thrasch" music and asking for contacts. "He sent a fan letter to Ian McCuy of DC Hardcore Heroes Fugazi. It read, Good Thrasch! So I was wondering, if you could give me some numbers or people to get in touch with, it would help. Thanks, Dave Grohl."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Accessible Live Shows
podcast.body: Fugazi was notable for hosting many all-ages shows with highly affordable ticket prices, alongside delivering emotionally intense musical performances. "Lots of all ages shows. Lots of shows were tickets cost practically nothing and lots of emotional intensity with their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anti-Commercial Practices
podcast.body: Fugazi was deeply anti-commercial, exclusively playing all-ages shows, owning their own label (Discord Records) to issue CDs just above cost, and maintaining the lowest possible concert ticket prices. They were also heavily involved in social and community activism. "They were completely anti-commercial. They played only all ages shows. They owned their own label and issued CDs at prices just above cost. They kept the concert ticket prices as low as possible. They were into social and community activism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anti-Moshing Stance
podcast.body: Fugazi, a post-hardcore and straight-edge band from Washington D.C., was one of the first groups to actively take a stand against moshing at their gigs. Adhering to their straight-edge principles of no drinking, no drugs, and respect, they viewed moshing as antithetical to their values. "The first band to really take a position against moshing was Fugazi, the post-hardcore band from Washington, D.C., who would have seen moshing culture... develop at the very beginning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commitment to DIY Ethos
podcast.body: The band maintained a total do-it-yourself (DIY) approach, operating their own label, Discord, and expressing contempt for the conventional record industry and its operational methods. "Plus they were totaled to do it yourself. They held the entire record industry in contempt and what had nothing to do with the way it operated. So they did everything on their own, through their own label, which they called Discord."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Confronting Moshers at Gigs
podcast.body: When mosh pits formed at Fugazi's shows in the 1980s and early 1990s, the band would politely ask the crowd to stop. In some instances, they would even bring an audience member who was moshing onto the stage, put them on the microphone, and instruct them to apologize to the rest of the crowd for their disruptive behavior. "Sometimes they would even drag a kid out of the audience, put him at the mic, and tell him to apologize to everybody for his bad behavior."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethical Standards in Rock
podcast.body: Fugazi formed from Ian MacKaye's previous projects, becoming a band centered on raw emotion. Beyond creating intelligent post-hardcore music, they established incredibly strong ethical standards that influenced the broader rock scene, defining anti-commercialism for many. "Not only has this band made some great and intelligent post-Hardcore music, their sense of ethics was so strong that they basically set the standard for all of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Emo
podcast.body: The band's approach and style would later serve as an influence for the emerging emo sound in music. "This would later take cues from bands like Fugazi when the whole emo sound came around a little bit later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Mogwai
podcast.body: Mogwai cites Fugazi as an influence. "They also like to cop ideas from Fugazi, and Kraftwerk, and Nirvana, and Electronic Offits like the Orb and the Apex Twin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

podcast.title: Major Influence on Dave Grohl
podcast.body: Fugazi served as a significant influence on the musical universe of a teenage Dave Grohl, representing the kind of music he "lived for." "Fugazi, a major influence on the musical universe of a teenage Dave Grohl."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Preservers of Traditional Emo
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, as emo diversified into various subgenres, Fugazi was credited with actively keeping traditional emo alive. "Sure, there was traditional emo, Fugazi made sure they kept that alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Screamo Band Dispreference
podcast.body: Fugazi's music was mentioned in contrast to what Screamo bands preferred, who opted for "old Joy Division and Smith records." This suggests a distinction in musical taste and potentially a different approach to intensity and political messaging between the groups. "They preferred old Joy Division and Smith records over Weezer and Fugazi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Standard Bearers for Emo Core
podcast.body: Fugazi not only defined the standards for emo core but also provided a centralized home for the genre through their label, Discord Records. "Not only did Fugazi set the standards for emo core, but they also gave it a home."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Ultimate Emo Band
podcast.body: Due to their profound ethical stance, anti-commercialism, and focus on raw emotion, Fugazi earned the reputation of becoming "the ultimate emo band." "And in the process, Fugazi became the ultimate emo band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Partners
podcast.body: Explosions in the Sky, a Texas-based post-rock band, toured with Fugazi. "They've toured with nine-inch nails, Fugazi, and here's that name again, Godspeed, New Black Emperor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

podcast.title: Unwilling Participation in Punk Revival
podcast.body: Despite their anti-establishment stance and likely disapproval, Fugazi found themselves unexpectedly drawn into the mainstream attention generated by the mid-90s punk rock revival. "They probably didn't like it much, but even they found themselves sucked into the mid-90s punk rock revival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Washington DC Origins and Straight Edge Philosophy
podcast.body: Fugazi, a band from the Washington D.C. area, was known for practicing "Straight Edge" punk rock, which advocates for a lifestyle free of drugs and alcohol ("No Drugs, No Boos"). "Another punk group who found themselves in Mortemand was Fugazi, a band from the Washington DC area that practiced a form of punk rock called Straight Edge, No Drugs, No Boos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Breakup and Formation of Fugazi
xref.body: The band eventually broke up, after which Ian MacKaye, a key member, went on to form Fugazi, a group noted for its focus on raw emotion. "Then Embrace broke up, Ian McKay went on to form Fugazi, a band that was all about raw emotion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Musical Development
xref.body: Dave Grohl began making music in his teens, progressing through a series of short-lived bands that were crucial to his development before joining Scream, then Nirvana, and eventually forming Foo Fighters. These early groups included Freak Baby, Fast, and Dane Bramage, as well as Mishmash Impossible, which notably opened for DC's Fugazi. "A Mishmash of short live bands that went nowhere but were very important to Dave's development."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of Fugazi
xref.body: After Embrace broke up, Ian MacKaye went on to form Fugazi, a band characterized by its focus on raw emotion and strong ethical principles. "Then Embrace broke up, Ian McKay went on to form Fugazi, a band that was all about raw emotion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influences

"The guys in Mug-Y are highly influenced by post-punk bands, like Jordy Vision, Sonic Youth, and my Bloody Valentine. They also like to cop ideas from Fugazi, and Kraftwerk, and Nirvana, and Electronic Offits like the Orb and the Apex Twin."

xref.body: Mishmash Impossible managed to secure an opening slot for the DC punk band Fugazi on one occasion, highlighting a notable early achievement for the band that featured Dave Grohl on drums. "Mishmash Impossible, who actually managed to get an opening slot for DC's Fugazi ones."

xref.title: Portage la Prairie, Manitoba to Global Punk Influence – Vegan Anarchist Politics and Fat Wreck Chords
xref.body: Propagandhi formed in 1986 in Portage la Prairie, Manitoba (population approximately 13,000), 50 miles west of Winnipeg. They built a reputation for strongly left-wing, sometimes anarchist, vegan politics targeting human rights violations, sexism, racism, capitalism, and organized religion. They aligned with American bands NOFX and Fugazi and were signed to Fat Mike's Fat Wreck Chords punk label out of California. Their debut record, *How to Clean Everything*, appeared in 1993. Still based in Winnipeg, they remain one of Canada's premier punk bands. "Very left-wing, sometimes anarchist, often vegan."
